short: A pool of money from many investors, invested by professionals in shares, bonds or other assets, with each investor owning units of the pool.
kid: Lots of friends each put a few coins into one big jar. A grown-up who is good at it looks after the jar for everyone. If the jar grows, everyone's part grows too.
detail: A mutual fund pools money from many investors and invests it according to a stated objective, such as large Indian companies or short-term government bonds. Investors receive units, and each unit's worth is the net asset value (NAV), calculated at the end of every business day. A professional fund manager picks the investments, and the running costs are taken from the fund as an expense ratio. Funds give small investors diversification, professional management and easy entry, sometimes from as little as ₹100 a month. In India, mutual funds are set up as trusts and regulated by SEBI, with an asset management company running them and a custodian holding the securities separately. A common confusion: a mutual fund is not a fixed deposit. Returns are not guaranteed, and the value of your units can fall as well as rise.
example: Say 1,000 investors each put ₹10,000 into a new fund, creating a ₹1 crore pool. If units are issued at ₹10, the fund creates 10 lakh units and each investor holds 1,000. If the portfolio later grows to ₹1.2 crore, the NAV becomes ₹12 and each holding is worth ₹12,000.

short: The value of one unit of a fund: the fund's total assets minus its liabilities, divided by the number of units outstanding.
kid: Count everything inside a jar that friends share, then split it by the number of friends. That tells you what one friend's part is worth today.
detail: Net asset value (NAV) is the per-unit price of a mutual fund. At the end of each business day, the fund values every holding at market prices, adds cash and accrued income, subtracts liabilities such as fees payable, and divides by the units outstanding. Purchases get the NAV of the day the money reaches the fund before the cut-off time, redemptions that of the day the request arrives. Because expenses are deducted daily, the published NAV is already net of costs. The most common confusion is treating NAV like a share price that signals cheapness: a fund with a NAV of ₹15 is not cheaper than one at ₹150. What matters is how much the NAV changes in percentage terms, which depends entirely on the underlying portfolio. ETFs also have a NAV, but trade on exchanges at a market price that can differ slightly from it.
example: Say a fund holds investments and cash worth ₹101 crore and owes ₹1 crore in expenses and payables. With 5 crore units outstanding, its NAV is (₹101 crore - ₹1 crore) / 5 crore = ₹20 per unit, so an investor with 2,000 units holds ₹40,000.
formula: NAV = (Market value of assets - Liabilities) / Units outstanding

short: The total market value of the money a fund or fund company manages on behalf of its investors at a given time.
kid: Think of a toy library that looks after toys for many children. Counting every toy it is looking after tells you how big the library is.
detail: Assets under management (AUM) is the total current value of the investments a fund, or an entire asset management company, manages for clients. It changes for two reasons: money flowing in or out, and market movements in the holdings. AUM matters because fund houses earn fees as a percentage of it, so it drives their revenue and is the headline measure of size and market share. In India, AMFI publishes industry AUM every month, and fund houses also report average AUM (AAUM), the average of daily values over a period, which smooths out month-end swings. A common confusion is reading rising AUM as proof of good management: a rally can lift AUM even while investors are pulling money out. Very large AUM can also make it harder for a small-cap fund to buy and sell without moving prices.
example: Say a scheme has 50 crore units outstanding at a NAV of ₹40, so its AUM is ₹2,000 crore. If it charges a 1% expense ratio and AUM stays at that level all year, it collects about ₹20 crore in expenses.
formula: AUM of a scheme = NAV per unit x Units outstanding
related: Association of Mutual Funds in India

short: The yearly cost of running a fund, shown as a percentage of its assets and deducted from the fund's value every day.
kid: A helper looks after your sweet jar and takes a tiny pinch of sweets as pay. A smaller pinch leaves more sweets for you.
detail: The expense ratio, called the total expense ratio (TER) in India, is the annual cost of operating a fund expressed as a percentage of its average net assets. It covers the investment management fee, distributor commissions in regular plans, registrar and custody charges, and other operating costs. You never receive a bill: roughly one 365th of the annual rate is deducted from the fund every day, so the NAV you see is already net of it. Small differences compound over long periods, which is why low-cost index funds and direct plans have grown popular. SEBI caps the TER by fund type and size, under limits it revises from time to time. A common confusion: the expense ratio is not the only cost, because brokerage on the fund's own trades is generally charged separately, and exit loads and taxes come on top.
example: Say you hold ₹1,00,000 in a fund with a TER of 1.5%: you pay about ₹1,500 a year if the value stays the same. In the direct plan of the same fund at 0.5%, you would pay about ₹500, and the ₹1,000 difference stays invested and compounds.
formula: Expense ratio = Total annual fund expenses / Average net assets x 100

short: A small fee some funds charge when you sell your units before a set period, deducted from the amount you get back.
kid: You promise to leave your toy in the shared toy box for a while. If you take it out too soon, you leave a tiny coin behind; if you wait, you pay nothing.
detail: An exit load is a charge levied when an investor redeems or switches units within a specified period after buying. It is expressed as a percentage of the redemption value and deducted from the NAV used to pay you. Many equity funds, for example, charge 1% if units are redeemed within one year, while liquid funds have a tiny graded load in the first week under SEBI rules as of 2025; the exact terms are in each scheme's documents. Exit loads discourage short-term trading that forces a fund to sell holdings and hurts long-term investors. In India, the exit load collected is credited back to the scheme rather than kept by the fund house. A common confusion is with entry load: SEBI abolished entry loads on mutual funds in 2009, so there is no charge for buying. Exit load is also separate from the expense ratio.
example: Say you redeem ₹2,00,000 worth of units eight months after buying, and the fund charges a 1% exit load on redemptions within a year. ₹2,000 is deducted and you receive ₹1,98,000 before any tax; had you waited past 12 months at the same NAV, you would have received the full ₹2,00,000.
formula: Redemption proceeds = Units redeemed x NAV x (1 - Exit load rate)

short: A way of investing a fixed amount in a mutual fund at regular intervals, usually monthly, through an automatic bank debit.
kid: Every week you drop one coin into your piggy bank, without forgetting and without waiting for a special day. Over time, all those small coins become a big pile.
detail: A systematic investment plan (SIP) automatically invests a fixed sum in a chosen mutual fund scheme every week, month or quarter, usually through a bank mandate. Each instalment buys units at that day's NAV, so more units are bought when prices are low and fewer when they are high, an effect called rupee cost averaging. SIPs build discipline, remove the need to time the market and let students and young earners start small. A step-up or top-up SIP raises the instalment by a set amount or percentage each year as income grows. In India, AMFI's monthly SIP inflow figure is closely watched as a sign of steady retail money entering equities. A common confusion: a SIP is not a product or a separate fund, only a method of paying into an ordinary scheme. It does not guarantee profits, and stopping a SIP does not sell existing units.
example: Say you start a SIP of ₹5,000 a month, investing ₹60,000 in the first year. With a 10% annual step-up, the instalment rises to ₹5,500 a month in year two, so you invest ₹66,000 that year and ₹1,26,000 over the two years.

short: An instruction to a mutual fund to pay you a fixed amount at regular intervals by automatically redeeming some of your units.
kid: You have a big jar of sweets saved up. Every week you take out the same small handful to enjoy, and the rest stays in the jar.
detail: A systematic withdrawal plan (SWP) is the mirror image of a SIP: instead of putting in a fixed sum regularly, you take out a fixed sum, monthly or quarterly, by redeeming units at the prevailing NAV. Retirees and others who need a regular income use it to draw on a corpus while the balance stays invested. In India, under tax rules as of 2025, it can be more tax-efficient than an IDCW payout, because each withdrawal is treated as a redemption and only the gain portion of the redeemed units is taxed, not the whole amount. The key risk is withdrawing faster than the fund earns: if withdrawals exceed returns for long, especially after a market fall, the corpus shrinks and can run out. A common confusion is to see an SWP as a guaranteed pension; the payout is fixed only until the money is exhausted.
example: Say you have ₹20 lakh in a hybrid fund and set an SWP of ₹15,000 a month. That is ₹1,80,000 a year, or 9% of the starting corpus, so if the fund earns less than 9% a year on average, the balance will gradually fall.

short: An instruction to move a fixed amount at regular intervals from one mutual fund scheme to another within the same fund house.
kid: You keep your sweets in a safe tin, and every week you move a few into a bigger jar that might grow. Little by little, all the sweets move over.
detail: A systematic transfer plan (STP) automatically redeems a fixed amount from a source scheme and invests it in a target scheme of the same asset management company on a set schedule. The usual pattern is to park a lump sum in a liquid or ultra-short debt fund and transfer it into an equity fund over six to twelve months. This spreads market entry, bringing rupee cost averaging to a lump sum, while the money waiting to be moved typically earns more than a savings account would. Each transfer is a redemption from the source fund, so it can trigger capital gains tax and any exit load there. A common confusion is thinking an STP works between fund houses or protects against losses: it only staggers the timing, and money already moved into equity still rises and falls with the market.
example: Say you receive a ₹6 lakh bonus, put it in a liquid fund and set an STP of ₹50,000 a month into an equity fund. After 12 transfers the full ₹6 lakh has moved into equities, each instalment buying at a different NAV.

short: Investing the same amount at regular intervals so you automatically buy more units when prices are low and fewer when they are high.
kid: You spend one coin on apples every week. When apples are cheap your coin buys lots, and when they are pricey it buys only a few, so it all evens out.
detail: Rupee cost averaging, known globally as dollar-cost averaging (DCA), means investing a fixed sum at regular intervals regardless of price, as a SIP does. Because the amount is fixed, it buys more units when prices are low and fewer when they are high, so the average cost per unit ends up below the simple average of the prices, as long as prices vary at all. Its real value is behavioural: it removes the urge to time the market and softens the regret of investing everything just before a fall. A common confusion is believing it guarantees profit or beats investing a lump sum. If markets rise steadily, investing all at once usually does better, because more money is invested for longer; averaging mainly reduces the risk of bad timing. It also cannot rescue a poor investment whose price keeps falling.
example: Say you invest ₹1,000 a month for three months at NAVs of ₹10, ₹5 and ₹10. You buy 100, 200 and 100 units, or 400 units for ₹3,000, an average cost of ₹7.50 per unit, while the simple average NAV over those months was ₹8.33.
formula: Average cost per unit = Total amount invested / Total units bought

short: Putting a large amount of money into an investment all at once, rather than spreading it over regular instalments.
kid: You get a big pile of birthday coins and put them all into your piggy bank on the same day, instead of a few each week.
detail: A lump sum investment is a single, one-time purchase, such as investing a bonus, an inheritance or the proceeds of a property sale in a mutual fund on one day. All the units are bought at that day's NAV, so the outcome depends heavily on the entry point. Studies across many markets find that, because markets rise more often than they fall over long periods, investing a lump sum straight away has usually beaten spreading it out over months. The trade-off is timing risk: a sharp fall soon after investing hurts more, and the regret can push investors to sell at the worst moment. Many therefore take a middle path, parking the money in a liquid fund and moving it gradually through a systematic transfer plan. A common confusion is that lump sums suit only equity; they are common in debt funds too, where entry timing matters less.
example: Say you invest a ₹5,00,000 lump sum at a NAV of ₹50 and receive 10,000 units. If the NAV rises to ₹60, your holding is worth ₹6,00,000, a 20% gain; if it falls to ₹40 soon after, it is worth ₹4,00,000.

short: The first-time launch of a new mutual fund scheme, when investors can buy units at a fixed starting price for a limited period.
kid: A brand-new shared jar is being started, and for a few days anyone can put coins in right at the start. After that, the jar stays open for everyone as usual.
detail: A new fund offer (NFO) is the subscription window when an asset management company launches a new scheme, similar in spirit to an IPO for a company. During the NFO, which SEBI rules as of 2025 cap at 15 days for most schemes, units are usually sold at ₹10 each. The money raised is then invested as per the scheme's objective, and an open-ended scheme reopens for continuous buying and selling at NAV shortly afterwards. Fund houses use NFOs to fill gaps in their range or ride popular themes, so NFO collections tend to surge when markets are hot. The biggest confusion is thinking an NFO at ₹10 is cheaper than an existing fund with a NAV of ₹100. It is not: the unit price does not affect your returns, and an NFO has no track record to judge.
example: Say you put ₹1,00,000 into an NFO at ₹10 a unit and get 10,000 units, while a friend puts ₹1,00,000 into an existing fund at a NAV of ₹100 and gets 1,000 units. If both portfolios rise 10%, both holdings become ₹1,10,000 (ignoring costs), so the lower unit price made no difference.

short: A fund that issues new units and buys back existing ones every business day at that day's price per unit, with no fixed end date.
kid: It is like a sharing club with an open door: anyone can join on any day, and anyone can leave on any day and take their part back.
detail: An open-ended fund has no limit on the number of units. When you invest, the fund creates new units at the day's NAV; when you redeem, it cancels them and pays you from its assets, so the fund itself provides liquidity. There is no maturity date, and the fund's size grows or shrinks with inflows, outflows and market moves. Most Indian mutual fund schemes, including almost all equity, hybrid, liquid and index funds, are open-ended, and you deal with the fund house rather than another investor. Because large redemptions can force the manager to sell holdings, funds keep some cash and may charge exit loads to discourage quick exits. A common confusion is with ETFs: an ETF is also open-ended in structure, but most investors buy and sell its units from each other on an exchange at market prices, not directly from the fund.
example: Say an open-ended fund has 1 crore units outstanding at a NAV of ₹25, or ₹25 crore of assets. If investors put in ₹50 lakh more in a day, the fund creates 2 lakh new units at ₹25, taking the total to 1.02 crore units.

short: A fund that sells a fixed number of units only once, at launch; afterwards investors can exit mainly by selling units on a stock exchange.
kid: A club lets friends join only on its opening day, then shuts the door. If you want to leave early, you must find a friend who will take your place.
detail: A closed-ended fund collects money during its NFO and then issues no new units. In India these are typically schemes with a fixed tenure, such as fixed maturity plans, and SEBI rules as of 2025 require closed-ended schemes to be listed on a stock exchange so investors can exit before maturity; at maturity, the fund pays out the NAV. Because the manager faces no redemptions, the money can be invested in less liquid assets and held to plan. The catch is that exchange trading in Indian closed-ended schemes is thin, so selling early can mean accepting a price below NAV. In the US and UK, closed-end funds and investment trusts often trade at persistent discounts or premiums to NAV. A common confusion is assuming the market price always equals NAV: for a closed-ended fund it is set by supply and demand.
example: Say a closed-ended fund's NAV is ₹12 per unit but its units trade on the exchange at ₹11.40. It is at a 5% discount to NAV, so an investor who must sell today receives ₹60 less on every 100 units than their underlying value.
formula: Premium or discount to NAV = (Market price - NAV) / NAV x 100

short: A mutual fund that invests mainly in company shares, aiming for long-term growth while accepting larger ups and downs in value.
kid: Your coins buy tiny pieces of lots of different lemonade stands. When the stands do well your pieces are worth more, and on bad days a bit less.
detail: An equity fund is a mutual fund whose portfolio is mostly shares of listed companies. Under SEBI's categorisation rules as of 2025, an equity scheme must invest at least 65% of its assets in equities (80% or more in categories such as large-cap), and sub-categories are defined by what they buy: large-cap, mid-cap and small-cap funds by company size, flexi-cap and multi-cap funds across sizes, and sector, thematic, value and ELSS funds by style or purpose. Equity funds generally suit goals five or more years away, as share prices can fall sharply over shorter periods. Returns come from dividends and price changes, judged against a benchmark such as the Nifty 50. A common confusion: 'equity-oriented' for tax purposes is a separate test based on the 65% rule, so some hybrid and arbitrage funds are taxed like equity funds while holding less net equity.
example: Say a flexi-cap equity fund has ₹500 crore of assets, so at least ₹325 crore must be in shares to meet its 65% minimum. If it holds ₹450 crore in shares and those shares fall 10%, the fund loses ₹45 crore.

short: A mutual fund that earns mainly interest by lending to governments, banks and companies, buying the bonds and short-term notes they issue.
kid: Your coins are lent to grown-ups who promise to give them back with a few extra coins as a thank-you. Most of the time, they do.
detail: A debt fund invests in fixed-income securities: government securities, treasury bills, corporate bonds, commercial paper and certificates of deposit. Returns come from interest income plus changes in bond prices, which move opposite to interest rates. Two risks matter. Interest rate risk depends on the portfolio's duration: longer-duration funds gain more when rates fall and lose more when they rise. Credit risk is the chance a borrower defaults; Franklin Templeton's decision in 2020 to wind up six debt schemes in India showed how this can trap investors. SEBI groups debt funds by duration and credit quality, from overnight and liquid funds to gilt and credit risk funds. Under Indian tax rules as of 2025, gains on debt fund units bought from April 2023 are taxed at the investor's slab rate. A common confusion is treating debt funds like fixed deposits: their NAV can fall, and returns are not guaranteed.
example: Say a debt fund has a modified duration of 4 years and interest rates rise by 0.5 percentage points. Its NAV falls by roughly 4 x 0.5 = 2%, so a ₹1,00,000 holding drops by about ₹2,000, although the higher yields it then earns help recover this over time.
formula: Approximate % change in NAV = -Modified duration x Change in yield

short: A mutual fund that mixes different asset types, usually shares and bonds and sometimes gold, in one portfolio to balance growth and stability.
kid: A lunchbox with an exciting treat and a plain sandwich. The treat is fun, the sandwich is steady, and together they make a balanced lunch.
detail: A hybrid fund invests across asset classes, mainly equity and debt, so that the steadier part cushions falls in the riskier part. SEBI's categorisation as of 2025 defines several types by their mix: conservative hybrid funds hold 10-25% in equity, balanced hybrid funds 40-60%, and aggressive hybrid funds 65-80%, with the rest largely in debt. Equity savings funds combine equity, hedged arbitrage positions and debt; balanced advantage funds shift their mix with market conditions; multi-asset funds add a third asset such as gold; and arbitrage funds are also classed as hybrid. The equity share decides both the risk and the tax treatment, so names alone can mislead. A common confusion is assuming a hybrid fund cannot fall much: an aggressive hybrid fund can still drop sharply in an equity crash.
example: Say you put ₹10 lakh in an aggressive hybrid fund holding 75% equity and 25% debt, that is ₹7.5 lakh in shares and ₹2.5 lakh in bonds. If shares fall 20% and bonds rise 2%, the fund loses ₹1.5 lakh and gains ₹5,000, ending at ₹8.55 lakh, a 14.5% fall.

short: A hybrid fund that shifts its mix between shares and bonds as markets change, buying more shares when they look cheap and fewer when expensive.
kid: When apples are cheap at the market, you fill your basket with apples. When they get pricey, you buy more bread instead, and switch back later.
detail: A balanced advantage fund (BAF), formally a dynamic asset allocation fund in SEBI's categorisation, moves its net equity exposure up and down, often within a band such as 30% to 80%, using a model based on valuation measures like the market's price-to-earnings or price-to-book ratio, sometimes combined with trend signals. To cut equity exposure without selling shares, many BAFs hedge part of their stock holdings with futures, keeping gross equity at 65% or more so the fund can be taxed as equity-oriented under the rules as of 2025. The aim is to buy low and sell high automatically and dampen the emotional swings of investing. A common confusion is to compare BAFs by name alone: models differ widely between fund houses, so two BAFs can hold very different equity levels at the same time. Look at net equity, not gross.
example: Say a BAF has ₹1,000 crore and holds ₹700 crore of shares, of which ₹300 crore is hedged by selling futures. Its gross equity is 70%, enough for equity taxation, but its net equity is only 40% (₹400 crore), so a 10% market fall costs it roughly ₹40 crore, not ₹70 crore.
formula: Net equity = Gross equity holdings - Equity hedged with derivatives

short: A hybrid mutual fund that spreads money across at least three types of assets, such as shares, bonds and gold.
kid: Instead of keeping only marbles, you keep marbles, stickers and shiny buttons. If one gets boring, the others may still be fun.
detail: A multi-asset allocation fund is a SEBI hybrid category that must invest in at least three asset classes, with a minimum of 10% in each, under the categorisation rules as of 2025. Typical portfolios combine Indian equity, debt and gold or silver, sometimes with international shares, REITs or InvITs. Because these assets often do not move together, losses in one can be partly offset by gains in another, giving a smoother ride than a pure equity fund. Fund houses differ: some keep fixed bands, while others shift the mix actively. Tax treatment depends mainly on the equity share, so check how the scheme is classified for tax. A common confusion is assuming more asset classes always means little risk: if the equity portion is large, the fund will still fall noticeably in a stock market crash.
example: Say you invest ₹10 lakh in a multi-asset fund holding 60% equity, 25% debt and 15% gold, that is ₹6 lakh, ₹2.5 lakh and ₹1.5 lakh. If shares fall 10%, debt is flat and gold rises 20%, the fund loses ₹60,000 and gains ₹30,000, ending at ₹9.7 lakh, a 3% fall.

short: A mutual fund that earns steady, low-risk returns by buying shares and simultaneously agreeing to sell them later at a slightly higher fixed price.
kid: One shop sells a toy today for a little less than another shop promises to pay for it next month. You buy it now, sell it later and keep the small difference.
detail: An arbitrage fund buys shares in the cash market and at the same time sells an equal quantity in the futures market, where the price is usually slightly higher. At expiry the two prices converge, so the fund locks in the gap, which broadly reflects short-term interest rates, whichever way the share price moves. The rest of the portfolio sits in debt and money market instruments. Because at least 65% is in hedged equity positions, arbitrage funds are taxed as equity-oriented funds under Indian rules as of 2025, which makes them popular with high-tax-bracket investors and companies parking cash for a few months. Returns rise when markets are buoyant and futures premiums are wide, and shrink when the gaps narrow. A common confusion is to see them as risk-free: returns can dip in some months, and costs and exit loads matter over short holding periods.
example: Say a share trades at ₹1,000 in the cash market and its one-month future at ₹1,007. The fund buys the share and sells the future, locking in ₹7 per share, or 0.7% for the month before costs, whether the share ends at ₹900 or ₹1,100.
formula: Arbitrage gain per share = Futures price - Cash price (locked in at the start, before costs)

short: A low-cost mutual fund that simply copies a market index, such as the Nifty 50, holding the same shares in the same proportions.
kid: Instead of picking your favourite sweets, you take one of every sweet on the shop's top-50 list. You get exactly what the list gets, nothing more and nothing less.
detail: An index fund is a passively managed mutual fund that aims to match, not beat, the return of a benchmark index such as the Nifty 50, Sensex or S&P 500. It holds the index's constituents in the same weights and rebalances when the index changes. Since no research team picks stocks, costs are low, and the main measures of quality are the expense ratio and tracking error. SEBI rules as of 2025 require index funds to invest at least 95% of their assets in the index's securities. Unlike an exchange-traded fund, an index fund is bought and redeemed directly from the fund house at the day's NAV, so no demat account is needed and SIPs are easy. A common confusion is to assume an index fund is safe: it falls just as much as its index in a downturn. It only removes the risk of a manager underperforming.
example: Say the Nifty 50 Total Return Index gains 12.0% in a year. An index fund tracking it, with a 0.2% expense ratio and another 0.1% of drag from cash and trading costs, would return about 11.7%.

short: A fund, usually tracking an index or commodity, whose units are bought and sold on a stock exchange throughout the day like shares.
kid: It is a basket holding a little of many toys, and you can swap baskets with other children at the playground any time it is open.
detail: An exchange-traded fund (ETF) is a fund, most often passive, that tracks an index, a commodity such as gold, or a basket of bonds, and lists its units on a stock exchange. Investors buy and sell units from each other through a broker during market hours at live prices, using a demat account. Large institutions called authorised participants, along with market makers, can create or redeem units in big blocks directly with the fund, which keeps the market price close to the indicative NAV. ETFs usually have very low expense ratios. The first US ETF, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF, launched in 1993, and India's first, Nifty BeES, listed in 2002; EPFO's ETF investments since 2015 helped India's ETF market grow. A common confusion: ETF prices can drift above or below NAV when trading is thin, so check the bid-ask spread and volumes, not just the expense ratio.
example: Say an ETF's NAV is ₹250 per unit but it trades on the exchange at ₹251.25. It is at a 0.5% premium, so buying 1,000 units costs ₹2,51,250 against an underlying value of ₹2,50,000.
formula: Premium or discount to NAV = (Market price - NAV) / NAV x 100

short: An exchange-traded fund that holds physical gold, so each unit rises and falls with the gold price without you storing any metal.
kid: Instead of keeping a real gold coin under your bed, you keep a ticket that says a tiny bit of gold in a safe locker is yours.
detail: A gold ETF buys standard-purity physical gold, held by a custodian in secure vaults, and issues units that trade on the stock exchange, so each unit tracks the domestic price of a small, fixed quantity of gold. SEBI rules as of 2025 require gold ETFs to keep almost all their assets in gold and gold-related instruments. Compared with jewellery or coins, there are no making charges, purity doubts or storage worries, and you can buy small amounts through a demat account. Investors without one can use a gold fund of fund, which invests in gold ETF units at an extra layer of cost. India's first gold ETF launched in 2007, and silver ETFs, which work the same way with silver, followed in 2022. A common confusion: a gold ETF pays no interest, unlike a sovereign gold bond, and it charges an annual expense ratio.
example: Say you invest ₹50,000 in a gold ETF and the domestic gold price rises 10% over a year. Your units would be worth about ₹55,000 less a small annual expense; if gold fell 10% instead, they would be worth about ₹45,000.

short: An approach where a fund manager picks investments and decides when to buy and sell, aiming to do better than the overall market after costs.
kid: Instead of taking every sweet in the shop, a clever friend tries to pick only the tastiest ones. Sometimes the friend picks well, and sometimes not.
detail: Active investing means a manager uses research, judgement or models to choose securities and their weights, departing from the benchmark in the hope of beating it. The extra return over the benchmark is called alpha, and the deviation from the benchmark creates tracking error, here called active risk. Active management needs analysts and trading, so active funds charge higher expense ratios than index funds. The difficulty is arithmetic: active managers as a group earn roughly the market return before costs, so after costs most fall short. S&P's SPIVA scorecards have repeatedly found that most active large-cap funds in both the US and India trailed their benchmark over ten-year periods. Results vary by segment and period, so compare a fund with its own benchmark over long stretches. A common confusion is judging a manager on one good year: consistency over a full market cycle matters far more.
example: Say a benchmark returns 12% in a year and an active fund returns 13.5% after its 1.5% expense ratio. The manager's picks earned 15% before costs, and investors kept 1.5 percentage points more than the index; had the fund returned 11%, a cheap index fund would have served them better.
formula: Simple alpha = Fund return - Benchmark return

short: An approach that buys and holds a whole market index at low cost instead of trying to pick winners or time the market.
kid: Instead of guessing which sweets are best, you take a little of every sweet in the jar. You never miss the best one, and you never have to choose.
detail: Passive investing tracks a benchmark, usually through index funds or ETFs, rather than selecting securities. The logic is simple arithmetic: before costs, the average investor earns the market return, so a low-cost fund that owns the whole market should, after costs, beat most active funds over time. John Bogle's Vanguard launched the first retail index fund in 1976, and passive funds now hold a large and rising share of global fund assets; in India, EPFO's ETF investments and the spread of Nifty and Sensex index funds have driven so-called passive flows. Passive does not mean riskless: it still rises and falls with the market, and choosing the index is itself a decision. Critics worry that heavy passive buying pushes money into the biggest stocks regardless of price. A common confusion is equating passive with forgetting your money; investors still need an asset allocation.
example: Say you invest ₹10 lakh in an index fund with a 0.2% expense ratio instead of an active fund charging 1.5%. Your yearly cost is about ₹2,000 instead of ₹15,000, a ₹13,000 saving that stays invested every year.

short: A measure of how much a fund's return gap with its benchmark index wobbles over time; smaller means it follows the index more closely.
kid: You try to walk exactly in your big sister's footsteps. If your feet always land right on hers you are tracking well; if they wobble left and right, that wobble is the error.
detail: Tracking error is the standard deviation of the difference between a portfolio's returns and its benchmark's returns over a period, usually annualised. For index funds and ETFs it shows how faithfully the fund copies the index; causes include expenses, cash held for redemptions, the timing of dividends and rebalancing, and trading costs. SEBI requires Indian index funds and ETFs to disclose tracking error and keep it within a set limit, under rules as of 2025. For active funds the same measure is called active risk, and a high figure simply means the manager is taking bigger bets away from the index. A common confusion is mixing it up with tracking difference, the plain gap in returns over the period: a fund can lag its index by a steady amount every day and show a large tracking difference but almost no tracking error. Check both.
example: Say Fund A trails its index by the same tiny amount every day and ends the year 0.3 percentage points behind: its tracking difference is -0.3 points, but its tracking error is zero because the gap never varies. Fund B ends the year level with its index but swings above and below it along the way, so its tracking difference is zero while its tracking error is positive.
formula: Tracking error = Standard deviation of (Fund return - Benchmark return); Tracking difference = Fund return - Benchmark return over the period

short: A company that runs mutual fund schemes, employing fund managers and analysts to invest investors' money for a fee.
kid: It is a team of helpers who look after many shared money jars for lots of families. For their work, they get a tiny bit from each jar.
detail: An asset management company (AMC), or fund house, manages investments on behalf of others. In India, a mutual fund is set up as a trust by a sponsor; trustees oversee it and appoint the AMC, which designs schemes, hires fund managers, runs research and compliance, and earns a management fee from each scheme's expense ratio. The investors' money belongs to the schemes and is held by an independent custodian, not on the AMC's balance sheet, so investors are protected if the AMC itself runs into trouble. Every AMC must be approved by SEBI, and several, such as HDFC AMC, Nippon Life India AMC and UTI AMC, are listed on Indian exchanges. Because revenue is a percentage of AUM, listed AMC shares tend to do well when markets and inflows are strong. A common confusion: buying an AMC's shares is not the same as investing in its funds.
example: Say ABC Asset Management manages ₹50,000 crore and earns an average management fee of 0.6% a year, about ₹300 crore of revenue. If markets lift its AUM by 20% to ₹60,000 crore, revenue rises to about ₹360 crore without a single new client.
related: Association of Mutual Funds in India

term: Association of Mutual Funds in India
hl: association of mutual funds in india
short: The industry body of India's SEBI-registered mutual fund companies, which publishes industry data and registers mutual fund distributors.
kid: All the shops on one street form a club. The club writes rules for good behaviour, counts how much everyone sells, and checks who is allowed to help customers.
detail: The Association of Mutual Funds in India (AMFI), set up in 1995, is the trade body of SEBI-registered asset management companies. It is not a regulator, since SEBI regulates mutual funds, but it sets codes of conduct, promotes investor awareness through campaigns such as 'Mutual Funds Sahi Hai', and works with SEBI on industry practices. AMFI publishes the monthly data that markets watch: industry AUM, category-wise flows and SIP inflows. It also issues the AMFI Registration Number (ARN) to distributors who pass the NISM certification exam, and twice a year it publishes the list that defines, under SEBI's rules as of 2025, large-cap (the top 100 companies by full market capitalisation), mid-cap (101st to 250th) and small-cap (the rest) stocks for fund categorisation. A common confusion is to treat AMFI data or membership as an endorsement of any particular scheme.
example: Say AMFI's monthly release shows ₹40,000 crore of gross purchases in equity schemes and ₹15,000 crore of redemptions. The net equity inflow is ₹25,000 crore, the figure headlines usually report; before investing through a distributor, you can also check their ARN on AMFI's website.

short: The version of a mutual fund scheme bought straight from the fund house, without a distributor, so it charges lower annual costs.
kid: If you buy apples straight from the farmer instead of through a middle shop, nobody else takes a share, so you pay a bit less.
detail: Every Indian mutual fund scheme comes in two plans that invest in exactly the same portfolio: direct and regular. The direct plan, required since 1 January 2013 under SEBI rules, carries no distributor commission, so its expense ratio is lower and its NAV grows slightly faster over time. You can invest in a direct plan through the AMC's website, MFCentral, stock-exchange platforms or many investment apps. The cost gap is often between half a percentage point and more than one point a year, and it compounds into a large difference over decades. Direct plans suit investors who can choose and review funds themselves or who pay a SEBI-registered investment adviser a separate fee. A common confusion: the direct plan's NAV is higher than the regular plan's, but that does not make it more expensive; it reflects cost savings already accumulated.
example: Say you invest ₹5 lakh in a scheme whose regular plan has a TER of 1.6% and whose direct plan has 0.6%. The 1 percentage point gap is about ₹5,000 a year at that value, money that stays invested in the direct plan.

short: The version of a mutual fund scheme bought through a distributor or broker, whose commission is built into a higher yearly fee.
kid: When a helper walks you to the farmer and helps you choose apples, the helper keeps a small share of every apple you buy, so you pay a little more.
detail: A regular plan is the route through which a mutual fund distributor, bank or broker sells a scheme. The AMC pays the distributor a trail commission every year for as long as you stay invested, and this comes out of the scheme's expense ratio, so the regular plan's TER is higher than the direct plan's and its NAV grows a little more slowly. You never pay the distributor directly, which is why many investors underestimate the cost. The distributor must hold an AMFI Registration Number (ARN), shown on your application. A regular plan can still be worth it if the distributor gives real help with fund choice, paperwork and staying invested during market falls. A common confusion is mixing up distributors and SEBI-registered investment advisers: advisers charge you a fee directly and are expected to use direct plans, while distributors are paid by commission from the fund.
example: Say you hold ₹10 lakh in a regular plan that pays the distributor a trail commission of 0.8% a year. About ₹8,000 a year goes to the distributor through the expense ratio, even though you never write them a cheque.
related: Association of Mutual Funds in India

short: The mutual fund choice where all profits stay invested in the scheme, so they show up only as a rising unit price, with no payouts.
kid: Your plant grows new leaves, and you leave them all on the plant. It keeps getting bigger instead of you picking leaves along the way.
detail: Most mutual fund schemes offer a growth option and an IDCW option, both holding the same portfolio. In the growth option, any interest, dividends and gains the fund earns are kept and reinvested, so nothing is paid out and the NAV reflects the full accumulated return. You realise gains only when you redeem units, and only then is capital gains tax due, which lets the full amount compound in the meantime. That makes growth the usual choice for long-term goals; an investor who needs regular cash can pair it with a systematic withdrawal plan. Because nothing is distributed, the growth option's NAV ends up higher than the IDCW option's once any payout is made. A common confusion: the growth option has nothing to do with growth stocks or growth investing; it describes only what the fund does with its earnings.
example: Say you invest ₹1,00,000 in the growth option at a NAV of ₹20 and get 5,000 units. If the NAV reaches ₹32 after five years, your holding is worth ₹1,60,000 with no payouts along the way, and tax is due only on the ₹60,000 gain when you redeem.

short: The mutual fund option, formerly called the dividend option, that periodically pays investors cash taken out of the scheme's value.
kid: Every so often you take a few sweets out of your own jar to eat. The jar has fewer sweets afterwards, because those sweets were always yours.
detail: Income distribution cum capital withdrawal (IDCW) is the option under which a scheme distributes money to unitholders from time to time, monthly, quarterly or whenever the trustees decide. SEBI renamed it from the dividend option with effect from April 2021 to make clear that a payout can come partly from your own capital, not only from profits. On the ex-IDCW date the NAV falls by the amount distributed, so your total wealth does not change. Under Indian tax rules as of 2025, IDCW is taxed at the investor's slab rate, with tax deducted at source above a threshold, which often makes it less efficient than the growth option plus a systematic withdrawal plan. Variants are IDCW payout, where cash goes to your bank, and IDCW reinvestment, where it buys more units. A common confusion is seeing IDCW as a bonus: it is your own money returned.
example: Say you hold 1,000 units of an IDCW option at a NAV of ₹25, worth ₹25,000. The fund declares ₹2 per unit, so you receive ₹2,000 and the NAV drops to ₹23, leaving units worth ₹23,000: still ₹25,000 in total, before tax on the ₹2,000.
formula: NAV after distribution = NAV before distribution - IDCW per unit

short: An Indian equity mutual fund with a three-year lock-in that has offered an income-tax deduction to investors in the old tax regime.
kid: You put some coins in a special box that stays shut for three birthdays. Because you agreed to wait, you get to keep a few coins you would otherwise have to hand over.
detail: An equity-linked savings scheme (ELSS), often called a tax saver fund, invests at least 80% of its assets in equities. Under the rules as of 2025, money invested in it qualifies for the Section 80C deduction, within the overall ₹1.5 lakh annual limit, for taxpayers in the old regime; the new default regime offers no such deduction. Each investment is locked in for three years from its own purchase date, the shortest lock-in among 80C options such as PPF or tax-saving fixed deposits. With a SIP, every monthly instalment has its own three-year clock. After the lock-in, units are treated like any other equity fund for capital gains tax. A common confusion is to invest only for the deduction and pick any ELSS in a hurry each March: it is still a full equity fund whose value can fall sharply, so fund quality and a long horizon matter most.
example: Say you are in the 30% slab under the old regime and invest ₹1,50,000 in ELSS in a year, under the rules as of 2025. The deduction cuts your tax by up to ₹45,000 before cess, and those units can be redeemed only after three years.

short: A debt mutual fund that invests in very short-term loans and securities maturing within 91 days, used to park spare cash at low risk.
kid: It is like a nearby cupboard where you keep coins you might need soon. They are easy to grab, and they grow just a tiny bit while they wait.
detail: A liquid fund invests only in debt and money market instruments with a residual maturity of up to 91 days, such as treasury bills, commercial paper, certificates of deposit and TREPS, under SEBI rules as of 2025. Because holdings mature so quickly, the NAV barely moves with interest rates, and returns track short-term market rates. Redemptions are usually paid the next business day, and many funds allow a small instant redemption. Individuals use liquid funds for emergency money and to stage lump sums, while companies park surplus cash in them. Under the rules as of 2025, there is a small graded exit load on redemptions in the first week, and gains are taxed at the investor's slab rate. A common confusion is treating liquid funds as risk-free: a default by a commercial paper issuer, as with IL&FS group companies in 2018, can cause a sudden NAV drop.
example: Say you park ₹5 lakh in a liquid fund for 73 days and it earns an annualised 7%. You would gain about ₹5,00,000 x 7% x 73/365 = ₹7,000 before tax.

short: A debt mutual fund that lends only for one business day at a time, so its value barely changes and its returns are low.
kid: You lend a friend one coin tonight, and they give it back tomorrow with a tiny crumb extra. Then you do it again the next night.
detail: An overnight fund invests only in securities that mature in one business day, mainly TREPS (tri-party repo backed by government securities) and overnight reverse repo, under SEBI's categorisation as of 2025. Because every holding matures the next day and is backed by government securities, interest rate risk and credit risk are close to zero, and the fund's return closely follows the overnight money market rate, which in turn stays near the RBI's policy rate corridor. Companies, brokers and investors use overnight funds to park money for a few days, for example between selling one investment and buying another. Returns are typically a little lower than a liquid fund's, since a liquid fund accepts slightly longer maturities, and there is usually no exit load. A common confusion is to expect overnight funds to beat a savings account by a wide margin; their appeal is safety and flexibility, not return.
example: Say a company parks ₹1 crore in an overnight fund for 10 days while it waits to pay a supplier, and the fund earns an annualised 6.57%. The return works out to ₹1,00,00,000 x 6.57% x 10/365 = ₹18,000 before tax.

short: A fund that lends for short periods, up to about a year, to governments, banks and strong companies, aiming for steady returns with little risk.
kid: You lend your coins only to the most trusted grown-ups, and only for a short time. They give them back soon, with a tiny bit extra.
detail: A money market fund invests in money market instruments: treasury bills, commercial paper, certificates of deposit, repos and TREPS. In India it is a SEBI debt category limited to instruments maturing within one year, under the rules as of 2025, sitting between liquid funds (up to 91 days) and longer-duration debt funds. In the US, money market funds are a huge parking place for household and corporate cash, and many aim to hold a stable value of $1 per share. In September 2008 the Reserve Primary Fund 'broke the buck' when its NAV fell to 97 cents after Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy, triggering a run that led to a US government guarantee. Flows into money market funds are watched as a sign of risk aversion or of attractive short-term rates. A common confusion is treating them as bank deposits: they are not insured and can lose value.
example: Say a money market fund buys six-month commercial paper at ₹97 that will repay ₹100 at maturity. Holding it to maturity earns ₹3 on ₹97, about 3.1% for six months, which reaches investors through a gradually rising NAV, less expenses.

short: A debt mutual fund that invests mainly in government securities, so it carries almost no default risk but swings with interest rates.
kid: You lend coins only to the government, which almost always pays back. Still, what other people would pay you for that promise can go up and down from day to day.
detail: A gilt fund invests at least 80% of its assets in government securities across maturities, under SEBI's categorisation as of 2025. 'Gilt' is a long-standing name for government bonds, from the gilded edges of the paper certificates the British government once issued. A variant, the gilt fund with 10-year constant duration, keeps the portfolio's Macaulay duration at about 10 years. Because the Indian government is very unlikely to default on rupee debt, credit risk is negligible, but interest rate risk can be high: when yields fall, long-duration gilt funds can post strong gains, and when yields rise they can lose money for months. Gilt funds therefore suit investors who expect rate cuts or can hold through a full rate cycle. A common confusion is equating government with safe from losses: the issuer is safe, but the NAV is not.
example: Say a gilt fund has a modified duration of 8 years and long-term government bond yields fall by 0.5 percentage points. Its NAV rises by roughly 8 x 0.5 = 4%, so a ₹2 lakh holding gains about ₹8,000, and a 0.5-point rise in yields would cost about the same.
formula: Approximate % change in NAV = -Modified duration x Change in yield

short: A debt mutual fund that lends mostly to lower-rated companies to earn higher interest, accepting a greater chance that some borrowers fail to repay.
kid: You lend coins to friends who sometimes forget to pay back, so they promise extra sweets. Most pay you, but if one does not, those coins are gone.
detail: A credit risk fund must invest at least 65% of its assets in corporate bonds rated AA or below, excluding AA+, under SEBI's categorisation as of 2025. Lower-rated borrowers pay higher interest, so these funds aim to earn more than high-quality debt funds. The cost is credit risk: if an issuer is downgraded or defaults, the bond's value is marked down at once and the NAV falls. Episodes such as the IL&FS default in 2018 and Franklin Templeton's winding up of six debt schemes in 2020 hit this segment hard and shrank it. SEBI now allows segregated portfolios, or side pockets, so a defaulted bond can be separated and any later recoveries passed to the investors who held it. A common confusion is to compare credit risk funds only by yield: a higher yield is payment for risk, so check ratings, concentration and the fund house's credit research.
example: Say a credit risk fund has ₹500 crore of assets and 4% of it, or ₹20 crore, sits in one company's bonds. If that company defaults and the bonds are written down to zero, the NAV falls about 4% in a day, so a ₹1 lakh holding drops by about ₹4,000.
